section.heading: 8.5. Constrained Maxima and Minima and the Method of Lagrange Multipliers
Constrained Relative Extrema
section.paragraph: In Section 8.3, we studied the problem of determining the relative extrema of a function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ without placing any restrictions on the independent variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ —except, of course, that the point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ lie in the domain of $$f$$ . Such a relative extremum of a function $$f$$ is referred to as an unconstrained relative extremum of $$f$$ . However, in many practical optimization problems, we must maximize or minimize a function in which the independent variables are subjected to certain further constraints.

In this section, we discuss a powerful method for determining the relative extrema of a function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ whose independent variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ are required to satisfy one or more constraints of the form $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ . Such a relative extremum of a function $$f$$ is called a constrained relative extremum of $$f$$ . We can see the difference between an unconstrained extremum of a function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ of two variables and a constrained extremum of $$f$$ , where the independent variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ are subjected to a constraint of the form $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ , by considering the geometry of the two cases. Figure 26a depicts the graph of a function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ that has an unconstrained relative minimum at the point $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . However, when the independent variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ are subjected to an equality constraint of the form $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ , the points $$(x,y,z)$$ that satisfy both $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and the constraint equation $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ lie on a curve $$C$$ . Therefore, the constrained relative minimum of $$f$$ must also lie on $$C$$ (Figure 26b).

section.heading: The Method of Lagrange Multipliers
section.paragraph: The major drawback of the technique used in Example 1 is that it relies on our ability to solve the constraint equation $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ for $$y$$ explicitly in terms of $$x$$ . This is not always easy. Moreover, even when we can solve the constraint equation $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ for $$y$$ explicitly in terms of $$x$$ , the resulting function of one variable that is to be optimized may turn out to be unnecessarily complicated. Fortunately, an easier method exists. This method, called the method of Lagrange multipliers (Joseph Lagrange, 1736–1813), is as follows:

note.title: The Method of Lagrange Multipliers
note.heading: The Method of Lagrange Multipliers
note.paragraph: To find the relative extrema of the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ subject to the constraint $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ (assuming that these extreme values exist),

list.item: Form an auxiliary function $$F\left( {x,y,\lambda} \right) = f\left( {x,y} \right) + \lambda g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ called the Lagrangian function (the variable $$\lambda$$ is called the Lagrange multiplier).

Solve the system that consists of the equations $$F_{x} = 0 F_{y} = 0 F_{\lambda} = 0$$ for all values of $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$\lambda$$ . The solutions of the system are candidates for the extrema of $$f$$ .
Evaluate $$f$$ at each point found in Step 2. The largest value yields the constrained maximum of $$f$$ , and the smallest value yields the constrained minimum of $$f$$ .

note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: A disadvantage of the method of Lagrange multipliers is that there is no test analogous to the second derivative test mentioned in Section 8.3 for determining whether a critical point of a function of two or more variables leads to a relative maximum or relative minimum of the function. Here we have to rely on the geometric or physical nature of the problem to help us draw the necessary conclusions (see Example 2).

section.paragraph: The method of Lagrange multipliers may be used to solve a problem involving a function of three or more variables, as illustrated in the next example.

note.title: Applied Example 5. Designing a Cruise-Ship Pool
note.heading: Applied Example 5. Designing a Cruise-Ship Pool
note.paragraph: The operators of the Viking Princess, a luxury cruise liner, are contemplating the addition of another swimming pool to the ship. The chief engineer has suggested that an area in the form of an ellipse located in the rear of the promenade deck would be suitable for this purpose. This location would provide a poolside area with sufficient space for passenger movement and placement of deck chairs (Figure 28). It has been determined that the shape of the ellipse may be described by the equation $$x^{2} + 4y^{2} = 3600$$ , where $$x$$ and $$y$$ are measured in feet. Viking’s operators would like to know the dimensions of the rectangular pool with the largest possible area that would meet these requirements.
